patient.name: Leo Okafor-Hughes
patient.complaint: Swollen, painful right knee after a minor fall (age 20 months)
background: Large bruises since starting to walk
Maternal uncle with prolonged bleeding after dental extraction
Lives with his parents in Croydon

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a boy, a deep bleed (haemarthrosis or muscle haematoma) after trivial trauma, a maternal family history and an isolated prolonged APTT.

points: Leo, **20 months**, brought in by his mum.
Right knee swollen and hot since a small tumble yesterday.
Refuses to bear weight; cries when the knee bends.
Big bruises on his shins since he started walking.
Mum's brother 'bled a lot' after having teeth out.

steps.lead: A boy with a **maternal uncle** who bleeds: an **X-linked recessive** clotting factor deficiency. Haemophilia A (factor VIII) is the commonest.
Leo has all three risk factors: **male**, **childhood** presentation and a **family history** on his mother's side.

points: Tense, warm, swollen right knee held in flexion.
Several large bruises on shins and thighs; no petechiae.
No gum bleeding; spleen not palpable.

steps.lead: Leo's swollen knee after trivial trauma is a **haemarthrosis**: deep bleeding into a joint, plus easy bruising.

steps.q: Mum asks whether this could be a platelet problem. Which feature points to a clotting factor deficiency?
steps.r: **Deep bleeding** (joints, muscles) means a clotting factor problem. Mucocutaneous bleeding (gums, nose, petechiae) means platelets or vWF.

steps.title: Haemophilia vs platelet or vWF problems
head: Feature
Haemophilia A/B
Platelet disorder / von Willebrand

steps.lead: Repeated bleeds would wreck Leo's knee; the deadliest risk is **intracranial haemorrhage**, so any head bump is treated as a bleed.

steps.text: Unexplained bruising in a toddler raises safeguarding concerns, but a swollen joint plus a maternal family history means **check a coagulation screen** first.
Girls are usually asymptomatic carriers. A girl with **Turner syndrome** (one X) can be a symptomatic carrier.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely coagulation result?' (prolonged APTT, normal PT and platelets) or 'diagnostic investigation' (factor VIII or IX assay).

steps.title: Leo's coagulation screen
steps.text: Isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets.

steps.lead: Leo's **prolonged APTT** with normal PT and platelets is the first-line pattern: an intrinsic pathway factor is missing.

visual.title: Leo's APTT
visual.label: Leo 72 s
visual.caption: Twice the upper limit. PT is normal, so the extrinsic pathway is fine.

steps.r: A **factor VIII assay** confirms haemophilia A; if VIII is normal, a factor IX assay confirms haemophilia B.

steps.lead: Leo's factor VIII assay comes back below 1%: **haemophilia A**. A normal VIII with low IX would be haemophilia B.

visual.title: Factor VIII level and severity
visual.label: Leo <1%
visual.caption: Severe disease: spontaneous joint bleeds. Mild disease bleeds mainly after surgery or trauma.

steps.text: Do not aspirate a haemophilic knee to 'rule out sepsis'. Afebrile, trauma, prolonged APTT: replace the factor instead.

management.exam: Expect factor VIII (A) or IX (B) replacement for a bleed, desmopressin for mild A, and immediate factor replacement for a head injury before imaging.

steps.q: Leo has severe haemophilia A and an acute knee bleed. Which treatment first?
steps.r: Replace what is missing: **factor VIII**. Desmopressin only helps **mild** disease; vitamin K fixes a prolonged PT.

steps.lead: Leo gets **IV factor VIII** now. Desmopressin is no use at <1%; haemophilia B would need **factor IX** instead.

steps.title: Acute bleed in haemophilia
nodes: Give factor first: VIII for A, IX for B
Then imaging if needed (CT head for head injury)
Rest, ice, elevation, analgesia (no NSAIDs, no IM injections)
steps.caption: Factor before scan: never delay replacement to wait for imaging.

points: Age 3: Leo falls off a slide and bangs his head.
Alert, crying, a small bump; no vomiting.
Mum rings the haemophilia centre straight away.

steps.lead: Leo's head injury is treated as an **intracranial bleed** until proven otherwise: urgent **recombinant factor VIII**, then CT head.
To stop bleeds happening, Leo starts **regular prophylactic factor VIII** and his family learn to protect his joints.

visual.title: Leo's joint bleeds per 6 months
visual.caption: Prophylactic factor VIII almost abolishes bleeds and saves his joints.

steps.lead: Leo's care runs through a haemophilia centre following **UKHCDO** guidance on factor replacement and prophylaxis.

steps.text: Mild haemophilia A before a dental extraction: **desmopressin** (often with tranexamic acid) can avoid factor concentrate.
Avoid **IM injections** and **NSAIDs/aspirin** in haemophilia: both increase bleeding.

science.exam: Expect X-linked recessive inheritance, why APTT is prolonged with a normal PT, and how desmopressin works.

steps.title: Where Leo's clotting fails
steps.caption: No factor VIII means too little thrombin, so clots are weak and bleeding continues.

steps.lead: Leo has an **F8** gene mutation from his carrier mum, so the **intrinsic pathway** cannot activate factor X properly.

o: Factor VIII is in the extrinsic pathway
steps.r: **PT** tests the extrinsic pathway (factor VII); factors VIII and IX are intrinsic, so only **APTT** is prolonged.

steps.lead: Leo's lab pattern follows from the pathway: **APTT** (intrinsic) prolonged, **PT** (extrinsic) normal.
Leo's platelets plug the surface fine, so no gum or nose bleeds; his problem is **deep bleeds** into joints and muscles.
Leo's cousin has **mild** haemophilia A: **desmopressin** releases vWF from Weibel-Palade bodies, which stabilises his own factor VIII.

steps.text: X-linked recessive: an affected man has **all daughters carriers, no affected sons**. A carrier mother: **half her sons** affected.

glossary.Haemophilia A: X-linked recessive deficiency of clotting factor VIII; the commonest haemophilia.
glossary.Haemophilia B: X-linked recessive deficiency of clotting factor IX (Christmas disease).
glossary.Haemarthrosis: Bleeding into a joint, causing a hot, swollen, painful joint with reduced movement.
glossary.Haematoma: A collection of blood outside vessels, e.g. deep in a muscle.
glossary.Haemophilic arthropathy: Chronic joint damage from repeated bleeds into the same joint.
glossary.Intracranial haemorrhage: Bleeding inside the skull; the most dangerous complication of haemophilia.
glossary.X-linked recessive: Inheritance via a faulty gene on the X chromosome: males affected, females usually carriers.
glossary.Carrier: A person with one faulty copy who is usually unaffected but can pass it on.
glossary.Turner syndrome: Chromosomal condition (45,X) in girls with one X, so an X-linked recessive gene can be expressed.
glossary.APTT: Activated partial thromboplastin time: tests the intrinsic and common clotting pathways.
glossary.PT: Prothrombin time: tests the extrinsic and common pathways; prolonged by warfarin and vitamin K deficiency.
glossary.Coagulation screen: Blood tests of clotting: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and platelet count.
glossary.Factor VIII assay: Blood test measuring factor VIII activity; confirms haemophilia A and grades severity.
glossary.Factor IX assay: Blood test measuring factor IX activity; confirms haemophilia B.
glossary.Intrinsic pathway: Clotting cascade arm involving factors XII, XI, IX and VIII, measured by APTT.
glossary.Extrinsic pathway: Clotting cascade arm triggered by tissue factor and factor VII, measured by PT.
glossary.Factor X: Clotting factor activated by IXa plus VIIIa; it converts prothrombin to thrombin.
glossary.Thrombin: Enzyme that turns fibrinogen into fibrin to form a stable clot.
glossary.Fibrin: Protein mesh that strengthens a platelet plug into a stable clot.
glossary.F8: Gene on the X chromosome encoding factor VIII.
glossary.F9: Gene on the X chromosome encoding factor IX.
glossary.Desmopressin: Synthetic vasopressin analogue that releases stored vWF and raises factor VIII; for mild haemophilia A.
glossary.von Willebrand factor: Protein that helps platelets stick and carries and protects factor VIII in blood.
glossary.Weibel-Palade bodies: Storage granules in endothelial cells that hold von Willebrand factor.
glossary.Recombinant factor VIII: Factor VIII made by genetic engineering, given IV to treat or prevent bleeds.
glossary.Prophylactic factor replacement: Regular scheduled factor infusions to prevent bleeds, mainly in severe haemophilia.
glossary.Mucocutaneous bleeding: Bleeding from skin and mucous membranes (gums, nose, periods), typical of platelet or vWF problems.
glossary.Petechiae: Pinpoint red spots from capillary bleeding, typical of low platelets.
glossary.Tranexamic acid: Antifibrinolytic drug that stops clots breaking down; useful for dental and mucosal bleeding.
glossary.UKHCDO: UK Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation, which writes UK haemophilia guidelines.

technique.stem: An 18 month old boy has a swollen, painful left knee after a minor fall while learning to walk. He has had large bruises on his legs for several months. His maternal grandfather had a bleeding disorder. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 120 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a bleeding toddler.

clues: swollen, painful left knee after a minor fall
steps.x: Boy, haemarthrosis after trivial trauma, bruising, maternal family history, afebrile; isolated prolonged APTT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: X-linked factor deficiency: **haemophilia A** is the commonest.

He is afebrile, and the APTT is prolonged.
That prolongs the PT, which is normal.
Causes mucocutaneous bleeding and is autosomal; joint bleeds and a maternal grandfather suggest X-linked.

steps.x: **A. Haemophilia A.** Rule: boy + joint bleed + maternal male relative + prolonged APTT = haemophilia A.

o: Normal APTT, normal PT, low platelets

technique.stem: A 6 year old boy has severe haemophilia A with a factor VIII level below 1%. He has had four knee bleeds in the past 6 months, each treated with factor VIII. He is well today.

Severe disease with recurrent haemarthroses.

Factor IX treats haemophilia B.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man with mild haemophilia A needs a tooth extraction. His factor VIII level is 18%. He is given desmopressin before the procedure.

practice.stem: A 3 year old boy has recurrent bruising and a swollen right elbow after a minor fall. His mother's brother has a bleeding disorder.

practice.e: A prolonged APTT with normal factor VIII and low factor IX is haemophilia B. A normal VIII assay excludes haemophilia A.

practice.stem: A 9 year old boy with severe haemophilia A has pain in his left knee after playing football. He cannot straighten the knee.

o: Normal knee with referred hip pain
Warm, swollen knee with reduced movement

practice.stem: A 19 year old man with severe haemophilia A hit his head falling off a bicycle 4 hours ago. He now has a worsening headache and has vomited twice. His GCS is 13/15. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 168/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Headache, vomiting, falling GCS and a Cushing's response after head trauma in haemophilia indicate intracranial haemorrhage, the most serious complication.

Head trauma, headache, vomiting, drop in GCS, bradycardia and hypertension.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man with severe haemophilia A has had many bleeds into his right knee since childhood. He now has chronic pain, a fixed flexion deformity and crepitus. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his knee problem?
practice.e: Repeated haemarthroses damage cartilage and synovium, causing haemophilic arthropathy. Prophylactic factor replacement prevents it.

steps.x: Cause of a chronic joint problem.

clues: many bleeds into his right knee
steps.x: Repeated haemarthroses in one joint, now chronic damage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemophilic arthropathy**.

elim: Acute attacks, usually big toe; no link to bleeds.
Symmetrical small joints, not one repeatedly bleeding knee.
Acute, hot, febrile; this is chronic.
Adolescent tibial tuberosity pain, not deformity in an adult.

steps.x: **B. Haemophilic arthropathy.** Rule: chronic haemarthrosis = joint damage; prophylaxis prevents it.

practice.stem: A 15 year old boy with haemophilia A fell onto his thigh at rugby. Over 6 hours the front of his thigh has become tense, swollen and painful; he cannot lift his leg. There is no fracture on X-ray. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.

practice.e: Haemophilia causes deep bleeding into muscles as well as joints. A tense, expanding thigh after trauma with a normal X-ray is a muscle haematoma.

steps.x: **D. Intramuscular haematoma.** Rule: haemophilia = deep bleeds into joints **and** muscles; give factor.
